planting.note: Surface-sow the tiny seed in spring on well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in a meadow, glade, or rock-garden setting.

directions: Surface-sow the tiny seed in spring on well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in a meadow, glade, or rock-garden setting, since this compact, non-spreading Oenothera stays tidy compared to its more aggressive relatives. Unlike many evening primroses, its inch-wide lemon-yellow flowers open in daytime as well as evening, drawing both day-flying bees and dusk-active moths, including specialist bees that visit only Oenothera pollen. It forms a low basal rosette with slender flowering stems and works well massed at the front of a dry native border. Deadheading is unnecessary, as seed capsules provide a modest food source for small birds through fall.

planting.note: Direct-sow onto dry, disturbed or gravelly prairie soil a few weeks before the last frost; keep on lean soil with reduced competition rather than in a rich, crowded bed.

directions: Direct-sow onto dry, disturbed or gravelly prairie soil a few weeks before the last frost, since this short-lived annual or biennial establishes quickly and often self-sows to persist in a planting once introduced. Small, bright yellow five-petaled flowers open for only a few morning hours through summer, closing by early afternoon, and are visited by small native bees and syrphid flies during their brief daily window. It is a pioneer species well suited to filling bare or recently disturbed patches in a prairie restoration while slower perennials establish around it. Because it is not competitive in dense vegetation, keep it on lean soil with reduced competition rather than in a rich, crowded bed.
